content: Classical swine fever (CSF), also known as hog cholera or pig plague (derived from the German term Schweinepest), is a highly contagious disease that affects both domestic pigs and wild boars. Symptoms Classical swine fever is characterized by fever, skin lesions, convulsions, and, particularly in young animals, death within 15 days of infection. The clinical signs of CSF are indistinguishable from those of African swine fever, making differential diagnosis essential. Epidemiology The disease is endemic in many regions, including large parts of Asia, Central and South America, and certain areas of Europe and Africa. In the United Kingdom, CSF was believed to have been eradicated by 1966, according to the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs. However, an outbreak occurred in East Anglia in 2000. In the United States, the disease was declared eradicated by 1978, as per the United States Department of Agriculture. Other regions considered free of CSF include Australia, Canada, Ireland, New Zealand, and Scandinavia. Virus The causative agent of CSF is the Classical Swine Fever Virus (CSFV), which belongs to the genus Pestivirus within the family Flaviviridae (formerly classified under Togaviridae). CSFV is closely related to other pestiviruses that cause diseases such as Bovine Viral Diarrhea (BVDV) and Border Disease (BDV) in ruminants. The virulence of CSFV strains varies significantly, leading to a wide spectrum of clinical presentations. Highly virulent strains are associated with acute disease, severe neurological symptoms, hemorrhages in the skin, and high mortality rates. In contrast, less virulent strains may result in subacute or chronic infections that can evade detection while still causing mortality in fetuses and newborn piglets. Piglets born to infected but subclinical sows can perpetuate the disease within a population. Other symptoms include lethargy, fever, immunosuppression, and secondary respiratory infections. The incubation period for CSFV ranges from 2 to 14 days, but clinical signs may not appear until 2 to 4 weeks post-infection. Animals with acute infections may survive for 2 to 3 months before succumbing to the disease. Control and Eradication Eradicating CSF is challenging. Current control measures focus on rapid detection and diagnosis, followed by preventive culling and, in some cases, emergency vaccination. Potential sources of infection include the widespread transport of pigs and pork products, as well as the presence of endemic CSF in wild boar and feral pig populations. Diagnosis Diagnosis of CSF involves a combination of epidemiological data, clinical symptoms, pathological findings, and laboratory tests. Diagnostic methods include: Direct immunofluorescence: Detection of the virus in histological samples. Indirect immunofluorescence: Identification of specific antibodies in serum samples. ELISA: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for detecting viral antigens or antibodies. The Philippine Hog Cholera Outbreak of 2007 On August 20, 2007, officials from the Philippine Department of Agriculture investigated an outbreak of swine flu in Nueva Ecija and Central Luzon. The mortality rate for swine flu was reported to be less than 10% in the absence of complications such as hog cholera. Earlier, on July 27, 2007, the Philippine National Meat Inspection Service (NMIS) issued a red alert for hog cholera in Metro Manila and five regions of Luzon after the disease spread to backyard pig farms in Bulacan and Pampanga. These farms tested negative for the swine flu virus but were affected by hog cholera.
